stories.headline: Fantasy football matchup rankings: Upgrade Tyler Warren, Tetairoa McMillan in Week 4
stories.summary: The most and least favorable matchups in the NFL for this week's games at the four key fantasy positions.
stories.body:
Making tough lineup decisions each week can be the most challenging part of fantasy football. When you're torn between two similar players, start the player with the superior matchup.

But exactly how does one determine the best (and worst) weekly matchups?

The matchup rankings provide a schedule-independent method to evaluate positional matchups, ranking all 32 opposing defenses in order of most to least favorable for opposing players at all four skill positions. Instead of relying upon seasonal totals, we calibrate points-allowed data to show how each defense fared relative to the difficulty of the schedule it has faced.

For Week 4, 2026 full-season data is used, but once five weeks are in the books, only the most recent five weeks' numbers will be used.

"Adj. FPA," or Adjusted Fantasy Points Allowed, reflects how far above or below players' weekly PPR fantasy point averages that defense held opponents at that position. A positive number means that the matchup is favorable; a negative number means it is unfavorable.

Finally, a caveat: Matchups are only one ingredient in my rankings formula. Not every favorable matchup should be exploited, nor unfavorable matchup avoided. If you want the most complete source for whom to start, consult our weekly rankings.

Quarterbacks

Matchups highlight: Jared Goff, Detroit Lions (at Carolina Panthers, Sunday Night Football). One the more quietly reliable quarterbacks, Goff joins Josh Allen, Brock Purdy and Tyler Shough among four with at least 16 fantasy points in each of the season's first three weeks. Of those four, he's the only one who hasn't been intercepted. Goff next faces the Panthers defense, which, aside from their 24-point Week 2 against the Atlanta Falcons third- and fourth-string quarterbacks, has been beaten up by the position. Caleb Williams (Week 1) and Deshaun Watson (Week 3) combined averaged 0.59 fantasy points per passing attempt -- the league average is 0.45 -- against the Panthers.

Others to like:

Trevor Lawrence, Jacksonville Jaguars (at Cincinnati Bengals)

Bryce Young, Panthers (at Lions, SNF)

Matchup to avoid: Jalen Hurts, Philadelphia Eagles (vs. Los Angeles Rams). He's off to a so-so start despite facing a favorable September schedule (WSH, @TEN, @CHI), due to inconsistent protection -- the Eagles rank 22nd in pass block win rate -- and a running game that hasn't fully launched (13th-ranked 110.7 yards per game, 19th-ranked 9.2% explosive run rate). That's of concern when Hurts faces the Rams, who rank second in yards allowed per passing attempt (5.2) and ninth in Total QBR allowed (53.2). Hurts' mobility presents his best case for a top-10 positional ranking this week, but aim to do better from that lineup slot.

Running backs

Matchups highlight: Aaron Jones Sr., Minnesota Vikings (vs. Miami Dolphins). Game script could be a big factor here, which is why Jones gets the nod despite pedestrian 3.9 yards per carry and 11.6 fantasy points per game averages. The Vikings are favored by 11.5, but the game has an over/under of 38.5. Over the past three years, there have been only nine teams favored by more than 10 with a sub-40 over/under. In those games, all nine won and their primary running backs averaged 14.8 fantasy points, 16.2 carries and 18.9 touches. Jones' 67% snap and 61% carry shares suggest he'll capitalize with fantasy RB2 caliber numbers.

Others to like:

David Montgomery, Houston Texans (vs. Dallas Cowboys)

D'Andre Swift, Chicago Bears (vs. New York Jets)

Matchup to avoid: Javonte Williams, Cowboys (at Texans). If there's a bright spot to the Texans' awful showing through three weeks, it's their run defense. The Texans have faced three of the first 16 picks in average ESPN drafts -- James Cook III (Week 1), Chase Brown (Week 2) and Jonathan Taylor (Week 3) -- and limited them to 3.7 yards per carry, an 8.9% explosive run rate and a 10.1 fantasy point average. Even in his breakthrough 2025, Williams delivered ordinary numbers when facing tough matchups, averaging 14.2 fantasy points in his five toughest assignments, so temper your expectations here.

Wide receivers

Matchups highlight: Tetairoa McMillan, Panthers (vs. Lions). He's coming off a brutal day against the Cleveland Browns, and largely CB Denzel Ward, in which he ran 45 routes yet garnered only five targets and 3.7 fantasy points. McMillan should find more open space against the Lions' secondary, which has already seen five different wide receivers score 11-plus fantasy points and afforded the position a fourth-best 2.05 points per target. CB D.J. Reed in particular has struggled, surrendering 39.4 fantasy points on eight targets in his 34 head-to-head matchups thus far, and he'll most likely match up frequently with McMillan.

Others to like:

Josh Downs, Indianapolis Colts (at Washington Commanders, Sunday 9:30 a.m. ET in London)

Michael Wilson, Arizona Cardinals (at New York Giants)

Tee Higgins, Bengals (vs. Jaguars)

Matchup to avoid: DJ Moore, Buffalo Bills (vs. New England Patriots). He returned from a shoulder injury to post a 38% target share and 12.7 fantasy point stat line against the Los Angeles Chargers in Week 3, but Moore has a much tougher assignment in the Patriots this week. Though CB Christian Gonzalez doesn't typically shadow the opponent's No. 1 wideout, and didn't in either of these teams' matchups in 2025, he's likely to see his most head-to-head matchups with Moore. Sure, Jaxon Smith-Njigba had a big score against the Patriots in Week 1 (26.2 fantasy points), but even with that score, Gonzalez and the Patriots rank 18th in fantasy points allowed per target to the position, and 20th in points per target to No. 1 wideouts.

Tight ends

Matchups highlight: Tyler Warren, Colts (at Commanders). He's averaging a serviceable 13.1 fantasy points per game, seventh best at the position, but Daniel Jones' inability to get anything done in the deep game has lowered Warren's ceiling (at least until Alec Pierce heals). Warren's 1.9 yard average depth of target is nearly four yards shorter than he had in 2025, but at least he should be able to rack up yards after the catch. The Commanders have afforded 20-plus fantasy points to tight ends in each of their first three games, have allowed the most points per target to the position (3.21) and have served up the second-highest yards after the catch average to tight ends (8.9).

Matchup to avoid: Mark Andrews, Baltimore Ravens (vs. Tennessee Titans). Between the healthy return of Zay Flowers and Andrews' own hand injury, which limited him to only 47% of the offensive snaps, the veteran tight end scored a season-low 5.4 fantasy points in Week 3. Things don't seem likely to improve this week, against a Titans defense that has been excellent against the position. Facing Kenyon Sadiq (Week 1), Dallas Goedert (Week 2, though shortened due to injury) and Isaiah Likely (Week 3), the Titans afforded the trio a combined 16.1 fantasy points, and 6.3 of those came on a Sadiq end-around rush.

stories.headline: 2026 MLB wild-card series Day 2: Live updates, lineups, analysis
stories.summary: Which teams will sweep and which will force a Game 3? We've got it all covered for you.
stories.body:
Who is ready for some more postseason baseball?

After an exciting opening to the MLB playoffs, it's time for four more games Wednesday. Will the Atlanta Braves finish off the the Philadelphia Phillies after a dramatic comeback win in Game 1? Will the New York Yankees knock out the rival Boston Red Sox? Will the Chicago White Sox sweep the Houston Astros? And can the Chicago Cubs turn on their offense after they were shut out against the San Diego Padres?

We've got you covered with pregame lineups, sights and sounds from the ballparks and postgame takeaways as each Day 2 matchup ends.

Key links: Mega-preview | Bracket | Schedule

Jump to:

PHI-ATL | CHW-HOU | BOS-NYY | CHC-SD

Philadelphia Phillies vs. Atlanta Braves

Atlanta leads 1-0

2 p.m. ET

Game 2 starters: Cristopher Sanchez vs. Tyler Mahle

What the Phillies need to do to force Game 3: Philadelphia has its ace going in Game 2 against Atlanta's Mahle. That's a big edge for the Phillies on the mound, and it's easy to imagine Sanchez dealing late into the game -- he has averaged more than six innings per start this season -- as they cruise to a win to even the series. They also have stars who can hit in big spots -- when J.T. Realmuto hit a triple in the top of the seventh of Game 1 to give the Phillies the lead, it seemed as if this series was headed in a different direction. That is, until Austin Riley's dramatic three-run homer in the bottom of the eighth. But Philly has still shown it has what it takes to win. -- Kiley McDaniel

What the Astros need to do to force Game 3: They need to play a more crisp game -- better at-bats and better command from their pitchers. They have the on-paper pitching edge with Hunter Brown starting and key relievers Josh Hader and Bryan Abreu more or less fresh after zipping through an inning each in Game 1. By contrast, White Sox relief ace Grant Taylor logged 54 pitches. Still, more than anything, Houston needs to generate more energy than it did Tuesday. The Astros looked pretty flat considering it was, you know, a playoff game. -- Bradford Doolittle

Game 2 starters: Sonny Gray vs. Max Fried

What the Red Sox need to do to force Game 3: For starters, scoring a run would help. And perhaps avoiding middle-middle fastballs to Ben Rice would do the trick. Beyond the obvious, though, the Red Sox need Sonny Gray to be who he was in his last wild-card round start in 2023, when he threw five scoreless innings for Minnesota. A lineup that was dead last in runs scored during September -- 71 in 24 games -- needs to find itself fast. Red Sox players exuded calm following their Game 1 loss, leaning on the previous holes this season that they've dug and climbed out of. This one, they know, is the most perilous yet: Max Fried on the mound, a Yankees lineup filled with left-handed hitters and 27 outs to save their season. -- Jeff Passan

By the time Game 2 rolls around, Morejon and Miller will be coming off three full days of rest, able to provide at least nine outs. No team scored more runs than the Cubs this season, and they'll have to show that against Nick Pivetta in Game 2. It will start, of course, with Pete Crow-Armstrong and Alex Bregman at the top of the lineup. King shut them down in Game 1, striking them out a combined five times. That can't happen again. stories.headline: NBA preview 2026-27: What Bobby Marks is watching at 30 training camps
stories.summary: As training camps get underway across the league, Bobby Marks examines roster, contract and fit questions for all 30 teams.
stories.body:
NBA training camps have officially begun!

Monday marked the arrival of media day for most of the league's 30 teams, with on-court practice beginning Tuesday -- exactly three weeks before the New York Knicks will raise their 2026 NBA championship banner.

We have you covered as you dig into the 2026-27 season, with roster breakdowns for all 30 teams, top storylines, decisions and lingering issues to watch over the next few weeks.

Atlanta Hawks

Contract snapshot

Guaranteed: 14

Partial/non-guaranteed: 1

Exhibit 10: 3

Two-way: 3

What to watch during training camp: the frontcourt

Despite the franchise's run to the Eastern Conference's No. 6 seed, Atlanta's lack of frontcourt size was a major weakness. The Hawks' defense ranked 18th in blocks and 29th in both second-chance and point paints allowed during the regular season. And in the playoffs, Atlanta trailed only the Denver Nuggets in second chance points allowed per game. Selecting forward Zuby Ejiofor at No. 23 in June's draft and re-signing center Jock Landale, who missed the Hawks' first-round defeat because of a right ankle sprain, will help. Mouhamed Gueye (fractured foot; might miss the start of 2026-27) and Henri Veesaar (torn right ACL; expected to miss the season).

Dates to watch

Oct. 19: Deadline to extend the contract of Onyeka Okongwu
Nov. 2: Deadline to exercise the third-year team option of Asa Newell

Extension candidates and eligibility

Gueye (four years, $95.5 million; through June 30)

Boston Celtics

Contract snapshot

Guaranteed: 14
Partial/non-guaranteed: 0
Exhibit 10: 5
Two-way: 2

What to watch during training camp: the offense

Over the past four regular seasons, Boston has won 73% of its games while also ranking in the top four leaguewide in 3-point attempts. But the Celtics' first-round loss to the Philadelphia 76ers revealed cracks in the NBA's second-ranked offense.

"The biggest thing is can we generate looks at the rim?" Celtics president of basketball operations Brad Stevens said. "Everybody wants to do that, and every one of us would prefer a dunk over a 3. Every single one of us. Those are hard to get, and we struggle to generate them."

With Jaylen Brown replaced by Paul George and Mitchell Robinson signed to provide frontcourt help, will the Celtics adjust their philosophy? Per Cleaning the Glass, George ranked in the 90th percentile among wings in midrange attempts. For his part, George also shot better than 39% on 3s for the ninth time in his career last season.

Dates to watch

Oct. 19: deadline to extend the contract of Payton Pritchard
Nov. 2: deadline to exercise team options of Hugo Gonzalez and Baylor Scheierman

Extension candidates and eligibility

Pritchard (three years, $69 million; Oct. 1-19)
George (two years, $125 million; through June 30)

Brooklyn Nets

Contract snapshot:

Guaranteed contracts: 15
Partial/non-guaranteed: 0
Exhibit 10: 2
Two-way: 3

What to watch during training camp: former first-rounders, playmaking and rim protection

The Nets drafted an NBA-record five first-round picks in 2025. For the roster to grow, there needs to be positive development in their sophomore season. Of the five former first-rounders, only Egor Demin averaged at least 25 minutes.

Brooklyn added 2026 No. 6 pick Mikel Brown Jr. and traded for Julius Randle, but did those moves give the Nets enough playmaking to the roster? In his freshman season at Louisville, Brown averaged 4.7 assists per game. And in the lineups where Minnesota did not play with a point guard, Randle averaged 5.0 assists per game.

The Nets also lack rim protection after starting center Nic Claxton was traded to Chicago as part of the Randle deal. Day'Ron Sharpe and Moritz Wagner, the only centers on Brooklyn's roster, averaged a combined 1.0 block per 36 minutes last season. The Nets allowed the seventh most points in the paint in 2025-26.

Dates to watch

Oct. 19: Deadline to extend the contract of Noah Clowney
Nov. 2: Deadline to exercise the team options of Demin, Nolan Traore, Drake Powell, Ben Saraf and Danny Wolf

Michael Porter Jr. (four years, $234.3 million; through June 30)
Terance Mann (three years $72.6 million' from Oct. 1 through Oct. 19)

Charlotte Hornets

Contract snapshot

Guaranteed: 15

Partial/non-guaranteed: 0

Exhibit 10: 1

Two-way: 3

What to watch during training camp: the backcourt and Brandon Miller

Coby White will assume the starting role after Charlotte traded former franchise guard LaMelo Ball to the Minnesota Timberwolves.

It should be a relatively smooth transition. White came off the bench in the 21 games after he was acquired from Chicago in February; but before the deal, he had started 97% of the games he played from 2023-24. And in the contests White played without Ball, the Hornets were plus-18.7 points per 100 possessions.

The Ball trade also was a bet on the development of Miller, who is currently rookie-extension eligible. Despite the 23-year-old forward needing offseason shoulder surgery, Hornets general manager Jeff Peterson said Miller should be a full participant in training camp.

What to watch during training camp: perimeter shooting

Is there enough spacing on this roster to allow Caleb Wilson and Matas Buzelis to develop offensively? Jalen Smith and Norman Powell were the only players on the roster to average at least 37% shooting from deep on a minimum of three attempts per game last season. The Bulls should get a boost with the addition of Buddy Hield. Acquired in a trade from Charlotte, Hield is a 39.5% career shooter from 3. During Tiago Splitter's season as the interim coach in Portland, the Trail Blazers finished third in 3-point attempts but 27th in 3-point percentage.

Dates to watch

Nov. 2: deadline to exercise team options of Noa Essengue and Buzelis

What to watch during training camp: frontcourt depth

Does Cleveland have enough depth if Peyton Watson, Evan Mobley or Jarrett Allen miss time? Allen and Watson combined to play 110 games with Denver last season. During the Cavaliers' postseason, frontcourt reserves Thomas Bryant (appeared in nine of 18 games) and Nae'Qwan Tomlin (appeared in seven) failed to reach five minutes per game. Because of the Watson acquisition, the Cavs have no financial flexibility to add a 15th player or even carry a non-guaranteed player. They are $45,000 below the first apron hard cap.

Partial/non-guaranteed: 2

What to watch during training camp: return of Kyrie Irving and health of Dereck Lively II

Irving hasn't played since March 3, 2025, when he tore his left ACL in a home loss against the Sacramento Kings. A healthy Irving will improve an offense that ranked 22nd in assists and 29th in made 3s.

Lively has played 43 of 165 games over the past two seasons. Lively hasn't played since November due to a right foot injury that required surgery in December.

"[Lively] has been working his tail off. He's in the facility constantly, completely locked into everything we're doing and doing everything in his power to be his best self," Mavericks general manager Mike Schmitz told Dallas Hoops Journal in August. However, as ESPN's Tim MacMahon reported, Lively has not been cleared for training camp and his status for the season opener is uncertain.

Dates to watch

Nov. 1: Moussa Cisse's contract becomes guaranteed

Denver Nuggets

Contract snapshot

Guaranteed contracts: 14
Partial/non-guaranteed: 1
Exhibit 10: 3
Two-way: 3

What to watch during training camp: bench depth

The Nuggets return the same starting five that captured the Western Conference's No. 3 seed, including three-time MVP Nikola Jokic and first-time All-Star Jamal Murray. Denver's questions start with its depth. The Nuggets re-signed Spencer Jones and added veteran DeMar DeRozan but lost Tim Hardaway Jr., Bruce Brown, Peyton Watson and Jonas Valanciunas.

Hardaway ranked fifth on the Nuggets in points per game, while Watson ranked fifth in minutes per game. Jones is the only Denver reserve to average at least 20 minutes per game on a team that won at least half of its games since 2022-23.

Dates to watch

Oct. 19: deadline to extend the contract of Julian Strawther
Nov. 2: deadline to exercise team option of DaRon Holmes II

Extension candidates and eligibility

Jokic (four years, $278 million; through June 30)
Cameron Johnson (four years, $144.7 million; through June 30)

Detroit Pistons

Contract snapshot

Guaranteed contracts: 12
Partial/non-guaranteed: 2
Exhibit 10: 2
Two-way: 3

What to watch during training camp: Jalen Duren's restricted free agency. Duren remains unsigned despite coming off a season in which he averaged a career-high 19.5 points per game and became the first player since Charles Barkley in 1988-89 to record four games with 30 points, 10 rebounds on 80% shooting during the regular season.

If an agreement is not reached prior to Thursday, Duren could sign the $9.6 million one-year qualifying offer and enter unrestricted free agency in 2027. No player selected to an All-NBA or All-Star team has ever signed the qualifying offer. If Duren -- who was named All-NBA and selected as an All-Star last season -- becomes a free agent next summer, eight teams project to have enough cap space to sign him.

Dates to watch

Oct. 1: deadline for Duren to sign the Pistons' qualifying offer
Nov. 2: deadline to exercise the team option of Ron Holland II

Extension candidates: None

Golden State Warriors

Contract snapshot

Guaranteed contracts: 12
Partial/non-guaranteed: 4
Exhibit 10: 2
Two-way: 3

What to watch during training camp: extensions, injury returns and frontcourt depth

Extension talks between the Warriors and Brandin Podziemski are a headline entering training camp. The 23-year-old guard is rookie-extension-eligible until Oct. 19. After Golden State extended Stephen Curry, it projects to have between $38 million and $55 million in cap space next summer. If Podziemski extends for more than $17 million -- the amount of his free agent hold -- Golden State loses financial flexibility.

Elsewhere on the roster, expect an updated injury timeline soon on Jimmy Butler III and Moses Moody; Butler tore his right ACL in January, while Moody ruptured his left patellar tendon in late March. Golden State was a plus-7.6 per 100 possessions when both players were on the court last season.

The Warriors extended Kristaps Porzingis and re-signed Al Horford. Even with both players returning, there are questions about the lack of frontcourt depth. And the health of Porzingis and Horford also is an area of concern, as the big man duo combined to miss nearly half of their games with the Warriors last season. (Porzingis is out indefinitely with a health issue.)

Unless coach Steve Kerr elects to go small with Draymond Green at the 5, Charles Bassey is the only other big on the roster. Bassey, a 25-year-old center, has yet to average more than 15.5 minutes per game, as he appeared in just 13 games last season between the Warriors, Celtics, 76ers and Grizzlies.

Date to watch

Oct. 19: deadline to extend the contracts of Podziemski and Moody

Extension candidates and eligibility

Moody (three years, $67.1 million; Oct. 1-19)
Podziemski (rookie extension; through Oct. 19)

Houston Rockets

Contract snapshot

Guaranteed contracts: 12
Partial/non-guaranteed: 2
Exhibit 10: 2
Two-way: 3

What to watch during training camp: playmaking

Fred VanVleet's season-ending knee injury that he suffered before 2025 training camp played a major role in the Rockets' offensive regression. With VanVleet on the court in 2024-25, Houston ranked 12th in offense and was 26-18 in clutch games. With the veteran guard recovering from a torn right ACL, the Rockets ranked 20th in offense and were 18-19 in clutch games. After electing to not sign a fill-in facilitator, Houston ranked 24th in both assist-to-turnover ratio and in turnovers committed. VanVleet's return and the free agent signings of Marcus Smart and Bogdan Bogdanovic should help the Rockets' offense operate more smoothly.

Dates to watch

Oct. 20: Isaiah Crawford's contract guarantee increases from zero money to $1.2 million
Nov. 2: deadline to exercise the team option of Reed Sheppard

Extension candidates and eligibility: None

Indiana Pacers

Contract snapshot

Guaranteed contracts: 14
Partial/non-guaranteed: 0
Exhibit 10: 2
Two-way: 3

What to watch during training camp: Tyrese Haliburton and Ivica Zubac

It is rare for a team that won 19 games the prior season to be considered a conference favorite. Indiana is different for multiple reasons.

The Pacers return 10 players, including All-Stars Haliburton and Pascal Siakam, from the roster that pushed Oklahoma City to seven games in the 2025 NBA Finals. Haliburton tore his right Achilles in Game 7 of that series and missed the entire 2025-26 campaign.

When Haliburton last played, the Pacers were plus-4.1 points per 100 possessions in the regular season and plus-7.8 in the postseason with their floor general on the court. He had 33 games with at least 10 assists and boasted a 5.6 assist-to-turnover ratio in 2024-25.

A healthy Haliburton will be tasked with reviving an offense that ranked 27th overall, 26th in field goal percentage, 20th in 3-point shooting and 18th in fast-break points -- while working alongside a non-shooting big man in Zubac.

Zubac, who was acquired from the Clippers at the 2025-26 trade deadline but played just five games with the Pacers, is 1-for-12 from beyond the arc in his 10-year career. Indiana likes to play at warp speed and kick out to shooters; its offense was ninth in pace even without Haliburton, while the Clips were 28th.

Date to watch

Oct. 19: deadline to extend the contracts of Haliburton, Siakam, Zubac, Andrew Nembhard, Obi Toppin, Jarace Walker and Ben Sheppard

LA Clippers

Contract snapshot

Guaranteed contracts: 15
Partial/non-guaranteed: 1
Exhibit 10: 2
Two-way: 3

What to watch during training camp: the backcourt and the final roster spot

Clippers coach Tyronn Lue has options for the starting guard spot next to Darius Garland, a good problem on the court after the franchise's tumultuous summer off of it.

Lue has started Kris Dunn in 126 of his 156 games as a Clipper, mainly because Dunn's high-level defense has been invaluable. And he has his 3-point shot, shooting 37.4% last season, his best in any season he attempted at least two 3s per game.

But LA has plenty of backcourt depth. The Clippers drafted Keaton Wagler with the No. 5 pick, signed veteran Bradley Beal and traded for Max Strus this summer. Last year's second-round pick, Kobe Sanders, started 16 games in 2025-26.

The Clippers must reduce their roster to 15 by the start of the regular season. They currently have 15 guaranteed contracts and Cam Christie on a non-guaranteed deal.

Garland (two years, $110.4 million; through Oct. 19)

Strus (three years, $63 million; through June 30)

Los Angeles Lakers

Contract snapshot

Guaranteed contracts: 16
Partial/non-guaranteed: 0
Exhibit 10: 2
Two-way: 3

What to watch during training camp: defensive identity

With 10 new players, expect a learning curve with the Lakers roster, especially defensively. That starts with new big men Walker Kessler and Sandro Mamukelashvili. Los Angeles ranked 20th in defense and 19th in points in the paint allowed last season.

Kessler has missed 101 games in the past two seasons, including all but five in 2025-26 with the Utah Jazz. But two years ago, Kessler held opponents to 48% in the paint as the contesting defender, fifth best in the NBA, per GeniusIQ tracking. (On offense, Kessler averaged career highs with 11.1 points, 12.2 rebounds and 1.7 assists with an NBA-leading 66.3% shooting from the field.)

Mamukelashvili played at his best when he was at the 5 and the only big on the court. In 2,159 possessions at center last season, lineups for Toronto ranked in the 89th percentile and were plus-9.4 per 100 possessions.

The Lakers also have 16 players on guaranteed contracts and will need to make a trade or waive a player by Oct. 12.

stories.headline: Ex-Man City chairman calls for club's directors to resign after Premier League guilty verdict
stories.summary: Former Manchester City chairman David Bernstein has called for the club's directors to step down after City were found guilty of serious breaches of the Premier League's financial rules.
stories.body:
Former Manchester City chairman David Bernstein has called for the club's directors to step down after City were found guilty of serious breaches of the Premier League's financial rules.

The league announced in a statement on Tuesday that City had been found guilty on all charges related to the period between 2009 and 2018, with league CEO Richard Masters saying that the club "systematically broke Premier League rules for nearly a decade."

City said in a statement on Tuesday that they will appeal the verdict.

"I can't think of a penalty strong enough for this, really. I mean, this is absolutely terrible," Bernstein, who was chairman of the club between 1998 and 2003, told talkSPORT.

"I want to raise another question, and that is the position of the board of directors. Because the directors of the club, including the chief executive, who's been there for years and went through this period, are responsible for the running of the club in every respect.

"If this was a public company of some sort, I think the directors, with something as serious as this, would have to stand down or be suspended pending the outcome of all this ... Appeal or no appeal.

"I don't think the present management can credibly continue."

Asked in a separate interview with the BBC whether City's actions constituted fraud, Bernstein suggested that he felt the actions of the board merited a legal investigation.

"I would go that far, yes," he said. "And if it is, -- I'm not a lawyer, and I'm only just putting this on the table as a thought, really -- but it is something that is so serious that it goes beyond the football authorities. It is damning beyond belief.

Bernstein, who is a lifelong City fan, also suggested that the club should be removed from the Premier League.

- Man City to appeal guilty verdict in Premier League breaches case

- Man City should be stripped of titles - Jamie Carragher

- Man City CEO says Premier League verdict part of 'conspiracy'

"If [City's appeal] drags on for a year or two, heaven forbid, that would be the worst thing for everybody," he told talkSPORT.

"But if it did, then you'd have a different situation. So it's a little difficult to predict. But all I would say is that money [a financial penalty] is not sufficient now.

"But if these charges stand now and let's say the appeal does not happen or fails, then I'm afraid for the club I love that they've got to come out of the Premier League. This is beyond awful."

stories.headline: Ayrton Senna's Honda NSX could fetch £800,000 at London auction
stories.summary: A 1991 Honda NSX that once belonged to Ayrton Senna will go up for auction in London at the end of October.
stories.body:
A 1991 Honda NSX that once belonged to Ayrton Senna will go up for auction in London at the end of October.

Chassis number T000233 was one of three NSXs delivered to Senna as part of his contract with Honda in the early 1990s and, due to its provenance, carries an estimate of £500,000 to £800,000.

When the car first went on sale in 1990 it had a list price of between £52,000 and £55,000, with low-mileage NSXs from the same era currently listed online for up to £135,000.

The legendary Japanese sports car is closely linked to Senna, who contributed to its development before it went on sale as Honda's answer to the more expensive Porsche and Ferrari sportscars of the era.

Chassis T000233 is finished in Formula Red over a black leather interior and was delivered to Portugal in March 1991 so that Senna could make use of it while staying at his property in Quinta do Lago.

According to the listing on Sotheby's website, the NSX featured in the 1992 documentary, 'Ayrton Senna: Racing Is In My Blood' and was used by the Brazilian to commute to the 1991 Portuguese Grand Prix in Estoril.

Senna, who died in an accident at the 1994 San Marino Grand Prix, won all three of his world titles with Honda power while racing at McLaren.

- Why is the Bahrain Grand Prix taking place in Malaysia, 4,000 miles away?

- Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia 2026: Race start time, how to watch

- Esteban Ocon to leave Haas but vows F1 career isn't over

He contributed to the latter stages of the development of the NSX, convincing Honda to stiffen the chassis and retune the suspension based on his recommendations.

The ex-Senna NSX, which comes with a fax from Honda confirming this car's original owner, will go under the hammer on Oct. 31 at Sotheby's London Auction in Belgravia.

stories.headline: Reeve laments Lynx 'don't quite have right group' after latest playoff flop
stories.summary: The Lynx became the first No. 1 seed in league history to be swept in its opening series, marking another heartbreaking playoff exit for the third straight year.
stories.body:
NEW YORK -- As the clock dwindled to zero in Tuesday night's first-round matchup against the New York Liberty, Minnesota Lynx standouts Napheesa Collier, Kayla McBride and Courtney Williams found each other on the Barclays Center court and shared a collective embrace, cementing yet another heartbreaking Lynx playoff exit for the third straight year.

Minnesota became the first No. 1 seed in WNBA playoff history to be swept in its opening series, losing 87-71 in a must-win Game 2 to New York. With the Liberty also comfortably winning Game 1, the games marked the first time in franchise history that the Lynx lost consecutive playoff contests by 15 or more points.

"We became a great regular-season team this year," coach Cheryl Reeve said, "and we ran into the wrong team."

Minnesota looked the part of title contenders for much of the season, improving to 31-7 in late August behind the stellar play of Olivia Miles, the unanimous Rookie of the Year, and Reeve's latest coaching masterclass, which earned her Coach of the Year honors for the fifth time.

But after a rocky past few weeks in which they almost fell to the No. 2 seed, the Lynx were for the second straight year unable to reach the WNBA Finals despite being the best team in the league during the regular season.

"I thought the playoffs would be hard for our team, regardless of who we were playing in the first round," Reeve said. "We probably needed a little better matchup to do some of the things that we did all season long, but that's not how it works."

Earlier this season, Reeve became the winningest coach in WNBA history and was inducted into the Women's Basketball Hall of Fame. She has led the Lynx franchise to four championships -- in 2011, 2013, 2015 and 2017 -- and nearly a fifth in 2024, when the team came one controversial foul call away from beating the Liberty in a championship-deciding Game 5 in Brooklyn.

But Reeve acknowledged Tuesday that while championships are in Minnesota's DNA, she hasn't viewed the past few years with a championship-or-bust mentality, particularly given those teams have arguably overachieved.

"There are sometimes when you have that team and that would be the case, you should feel that way," Reeve said. "I have not felt like we've had that team over these three years, and so what we're doing is sort of maybe exceeding expectations in the regular season, and then when it comes playoffs, maybe we don't quite have the right group to be effective.

"I just know we have some work to do. I have to help us. I have to get us the appropriate help to do it, make the hard decisions to do that. I couldn't get us there in this series, and so it's on me. I have to help them win in the playoffs ... both as an executive [president of basketball operations] and as the coach, and I'll find a way to do that."

Asked why it has been difficult to translate regular-season success to winning championships, Collier -- the Lynx's perennial MVP candidate who returned midseason after offseason ankle surgeries -- said she wasn't sure what to attribute that to.

"I don't know. I feel like if we knew the answer to that, we would be translating it over," Collier said. "That's something that obviously we have to figure out."

Granted, the Lynx's matchup against New York was an unfavorable one: The Liberty are known for their length at nearly every position, even bringing 6-foot-11 Han Xu off the bench, and their prowess at defending the rim. Reeve pointed to New York's ability to "render ineffective" both Miles, who typically thrives around the basket, and All-Star forward Natasha Howard as Minnesota's undoing.

"I think their size really bothered us," Miles said. "We didn't really know what coverage worked best. We were switching, we were hedging, we were playing drop, trying to throw a lot of things at them. Their size really is imposing."

New York also wasn't a traditional No. 8 seed -- seven games separated Minnesota and New York in the standings and only two separated the No. 5 and No. 8 seeds. The Liberty's big three of Breanna Stewart, Jonquel Jones and Sabrina Ionescu scored or assisted on 70 points for New York, whereas the Lynx had 71 as a team.

Meanwhile, Collier didn't look like her assertive, dominant self this series. On Tuesday, she got into foul trouble in the third quarter, making a late rally more difficult. And Miles, who so often played beyond her years this summer, looked like a rookie playing in her first postseason games.

"Their big three were really, really good," Reeve said, "and we kind of struggled to have a big three. That's just not a great place to be."

Said Miles: "You could tell for a lot of us that we're playing tight and stressed and afraid of losing instead of trying to win. Maybe from my end, that's a lack of experience. But I think we wanted to win so bad that we almost cared too much, honestly, and cared in the wrong ways, and it really limited us."

Miles finished the series with totals of 16 points, two assists, five turnovers and seven fouls. It was what Reeve said can be a learning experience for her but one that doesn't erase her body of work this season.

"Everyone wants to win all the time. That's just not how it works," Miles said. "Sometimes I have to have experiences like this that hurt this bad to get me to where I want to be."

Minnesota faces a fascinating offseason ahead with Williams, McBride and Howard all under contract through 2027, plus Miles still on her rookie deal. Collier, meanwhile, will hit free agency and cannot be cored by the team. She has been noncommittal when asked about her desire to stay with Minnesota beyond this year.

Time will tell whether that moment with Collier, McBride and Williams embracing on the Barclays Court, with a WNBA championship out of reach once more, will be the lasting image of the Lynx as we know it.

"We got to each other at special times in our career," McBride said of the trio. "What we've created in Minnesota, our culture, when people come into it, they love it. They love being a part of what we've been able to grow these last couple years, and that's not lost on me."

stories.headline: Former draftee slams AFL over concussion plight
stories.summary: An AFL draftee whose life was upended by a concussion injury says he "was so close to ending everything".
stories.body:
An AFL draftee whose life was upended by a concussion injury says he "was so close to ending everything".

Aiden O'Driscoll, who had to retire because of a devastating training injury without making his AFL debut, also slammed the league as an "absolute joke".

"The last couple of years I've experienced nothing but pain, and I've explained it multiple times to you. You're supposed to help AFL players through hardship, not leave them with absolutely nothing," O'Driscoll wrote in his extensive Instagram post.

His comments came a day after Geelong announced defender Jake Kolodjashnij had retired.

Last month, the Cats were fined $140,000 and current AFL chairman Craig Drummond apologised after it emerged the club had agreed to a secret concussion waiver with Kolodjashnij. Drummond was Geelong president at the time the agreement was struck.

The Geelong controversy highlighted the complexity and sensitivity around contact sport's concussion crisis.

The Western Bulldogs recruited O'Driscoll in the 2023 draft. But a head injury that summer left him with significant ongoing health problems and the club announced in May, 2024 that he had retired on medical grounds.

"The doctors described my concussion as 'one of the worst' they've seen, with eight micro brain bleeds, and (a) fracture behind my ear," O'Driscoll wrote.

"From a medical point of view, losing my career, my identity plus going through the symptoms I have, you'd think the AFL would be useful with some support?

O'Driscoll added it took the AFL six weeks to find him a psychologist.

"Through this period, I was grieving the most, it got to the point where I started questioning my life? If it was worth living?," he wrote.

"I was so close to ending everything, I would've been free from all the pain/trauma. My family/close friends and partners honestly kept me here."

Melbourne premiership player Angus Brayshaw also had to retire in 2024 because of his concussion issues.

In his emotional toast to other retiring players at the Brownlow Medal function that year, Brayshaw referred to O'Driscoll by name.

"I know a few other past players that are dealing with the same issues as I am," O'Driscoll said.

"AFL it's time to step up! I'm a 21-year-old that can't keep suffering each week. While you're at it, help the other past players that need support."

O'Driscoll added he had been told at 18 never to play contact sport again.

The AFL and the players' association were contacted for comment.

stories.headline: NRL Midweek Mail Grand Final: Halves injuries put Brooks on Penrith's radar
stories.summary: Daniel Tupou insists the result of the Grand Final will not decide whether he plays on, while Robert Toia is modest about his extraordinary talents.
stories.body:
The NRL rarely stands still.

Between training sessions, media appearances, and behind-the-scenes conversations, new storylines often begin to emerge before the weekend arrives.

Throughout the week, ESPN will be gathering notes, insights, and updates from around the competition heading into the NRL's Grand Final weekend.

Panthers emerge in Brooks race

Penrith have emerged as a potential destination for Luke Brooks should the veteran half depart Manly ahead of the 2027 season.

ESPN understands the Panthers are interested in Brooks, per multiple sources, as uncertainty continues around the playmaker's future at the Sea Eagles.

Brooks remains contracted to Manly through 2027, meaning any move for next season would require an early release, with Jamal Fogarty and highly rated youngster Joey Walsh the focus of the Sea Eagles' halves plans.

The Penrith link comes amid uncertainty surrounding their halves stocks for 2027.

Nathan Cleary and Blaize Talagi face lengthy injury recoveries, while Jack Cole will depart for the Perth Bears at season's end, leaving Jack Cogger as the Panthers' other established halves option.

Raiders eye Storm young gun

Canberra are keeping tabs on Melbourne Storm prop Josiah Pahulu ahead of the November 1 transfer window.

ESPN understands the Raiders are interested in the highly rated 22-year-old, who remains contracted to Melbourne through the end of 2027.

Pahulu joined the Storm from the Gold Coast midway through 2025 and has since continued his development in Melbourne's system.

Eligible to negotiate with rival clubs for 2028 from November 1, Pahulu has emerged as a player of interest for Canberra as clubs begin positioning themselves ahead of the market opening.

Amone commits to the Dragons

St George Illawarra have retained promising youngster Viliami Amone on a one-year deal for 2027 despite interest from several rival clubs, ESPN understands.

The younger brother of former Dragons playmaker Junior Amone was part of the club's Jersey Flegg side that claimed the 2026 minor premiership.

He played in the second row during the season and also earned four NSW Cup appearances as he progressed through the Dragons' pathways.

Tupou says Grand Final result won't decide his future

Daniel Tupou has put talks over his playing future on hold until after Sunday's Grand Final, but says the result will have no bearing on whether he continues next season.

Asked if winning a premiership might change his decision, the 35-year-old said:

"Not at all. I've just parked it for now in this finals series. Once this game's done, then I'll get back onto it."

Tupou said he still believes he has another year in him and confirmed family and friends have encouraged him to keep playing. For now, his focus is on a fourth Grand Final appearance with the Roosters.

Toia rejects top-three centre talk ahead of grand final

Robert Toia has played his way into conversations about the NRL's best centres, but the Roosters youngster believes a top-three ranking is premature.

"It's pretty good to hear, to be honest," Toia said of the praise.

"But I think that's exaggerated. I wouldn't say I'm a top-three centre.

"I feel like I've been playing somewhat good footy, but there's still a lot to show and still more to come."

Sunday's Grand Final offers a test against Bradman Best, whom Toia named among the most difficult centres to defend because of his size, speed and agility.

The pair have never met off the field, but Toia said he loves the matchup and is looking forward to measuring himself against the Newcastle star.

Familiar faces on the other side

Tupou said the Roosters are pleased to see former teammate Sandon Smith thriving at Newcastle, praising him as a player who delivered in big games during his time at the club. That goodwill will be set aside on Sunday.

Tupou is also preparing to face Dom Young, whose return to the Knights has set up a direct contest with his former Roosters teammate.

He said he did not know the details behind Young's exit and declined to speculate, but expects "a great battle" against the winger.

stories.headline: NFL Week 4 latest intel, buzz questions, news, fantasy tips
stories.summary: Alarm bells for Justin Herbert and Drake Maye? More QB trades on the way? Growing injury concerns for the 49ers and Panthers? Here's the latest for Week 4.
stories.body:
We're onto Week 4 of the 2026 NFL season, and insiders Jeremy Fowler and Dan Graziano have been making calls to sources around the league for the latest news and notable buzz.

Drake Maye and the Patriots had an ugly game Sunday, but Maye is hardly the only quarterback with a concerning start to the season. Dan and Jeremy asked around the league to get a sense of which QBs land on the early-season panic meter. And after J.J. McCarthy kicked off trading season Monday in going to the Giants, our insiders poked around on more QB trades that could be on deck. Any other passers potentially switching teams?

Additionally, is the league buying the 3-0 start from the Raiders, who have already matched their win total from 2025? Can Las Vegas keep this up? And which teams -- 3-0 or otherwise -- are getting hit particularly hard with injuries? It's all here, as Jeremy and Dan answer big questions, hand out useful fantasy football nuggets and empty their reporting notebooks heading into Week 4.

Jump to:

QB panic meter | QB trades

Raiders' start | Injury impact

Fantasy football advice

Which QB currently sits atop the league's panic meter?
Fowler: Three come to mind here -- Drake Maye, Cam Ward and Justin Herbert. All three garner varying degrees of panic, but I'm putting Maye on top for now. The Year 3 regression is startling. He looks shaken right now. Mike Vrabel's comment after the 35-6 loss to Jacksonville was blunt: "My concern level is very high for this football team." Maye is a big part of that after six interceptions in three games. The next day, Vrabel questioned whether the Patriots' offense needs to scale back its game plans a bit, essentially to do less but do it better.

Still, the notion that Maye's play can improve is there. He was considered one of the cleanest quarterback prospects of the past half-decade when he entered the 2024 draft. He played at an MVP level less than a calendar year ago. And to be sure, the Patriots have not played well around Maye and have not adequately protected him, and wide receiver A.J. Brown's absence is deeply felt. The passing game was designed to feed him the ball often. Josh McDaniels' scheme is also considered to be complex for young passers.

But dating to last year's playoffs, Maye's seven-game production line is 120-of-200 passing for 1,413 yards, seven touchdowns and 10 interceptions. Those are 1970s QB numbers -- and jarring for a quarterback seemingly on the door of superstardom (to be fair, four of those seven were playoff games against top-shelf defenses).

So, I'm leaving the door open for Maye to fix it, but the panic can be found in Vrabel's voice right now. I mean, this team was in the Super Bowl last season, so the expectations couldn't have been higher. Perhaps last season's soft schedule masked a quarterback who was still very much in development.

Graziano: It went largely unnoticed during their run to the Super Bowl, but Maye did not play well during the playoffs last season. And many of the issues that surfaced then have carried into this season. What I'm hearing is that it's not that Maye is a consistently poor decision-maker, it's that he's an occasionally disastrous one, and the mistakes are exceedingly harmful. Through three quarters of the season opener in Seattle, you'd have said Maye was playing well, demonstrating poise in difficult circumstances and putting his team in position to win. Then he fell apart completely in the fourth quarter.

There are ups and downs with young players, but Maye's downs have been way too far down. And without Brown, the Patriots don't have enough around Maye to overcome the errors. His protection also hasn't been consistent. But while I don't get the sense that people think Maye has regressed, there is concern that we aren't seeing advancement in some of the young-player areas that should be improving for a quarterback who finished second in MVP voting and played in the Super Bowl.

Fowler: After some conversations this week, I feel certain that Tennessee wants to give Ward more time despite his 3-17 record as a starter. Accuracy and decision-making are issues, but the Titans hope he will build off the late-game growing pains. He also isn't turning the ball over at a high clip (one interception through three games) and the team values his makeup and work ethic. Adjusting to Brian Daboll's offense has taken time, but averaging 12 points can test a front office's -- and locker room's -- patience only for so long.

Graziano: The sense I get from Tennessee is that things are out of whack there and haven't gotten on track at all. I'm talking about the overall environment around the team, not just Ward. There's an obvious disconnect between Ward and the coaching staff, or at least the scheme, and the time to address and adjust those things was the spring and summer. How do the Titans fix lingering structural issues with their offense and with Ward's development during the season? There's still widespread belief that Ward has the character and the ability to weather early-career struggles and come out stronger for it. But there's also a sense around the league that it should look better than it does right now, and there's curiosity about what's preventing the improvement from happening.

Fowler: Jumping to Herbert, his play is inexcusably bad, but he's in Year 7 with 98 career starts, with most of those played at a high level. He has proof of concept more so than Maye or Ward. The jumbled offense under offensive coordinator Mike McDaniel hasn't helped. And I'm not exactly sure where they turn next.

Graziano: Yikes. Talk about disconnect between player and scheme. Everything looks "difficult and exhausting" for Herbert, using the words of one evaluator I spoke to last week. There was so much talk in the offseason about how Herbert and his immense natural talent would flourish under McDaniel, but it's clearly not clicking. A fresh wave of offensive line injuries that happened as the season was getting underway certainly didn't help. But the run game can't get going, the receivers haven't taken the jumps we were promised, and Herbert has looked confused and overwhelmed by whatever it is he's being asked to do out there.

A lot of people have theories on what the Chargers need to do in terms of simplifying things so they can just start having success to build on. But there's also concern that the personnel doesn't fit what the offense is built to do, which might be difficult to overcome.

Fowler: Next up for the Chargers: at Seattle, vs. Denver, at Kansas City, then a much-needed bye before the Rams, Texans and Ravens await. Oof. Not many get-right games on that schedule.

Look, Herbert has excelled as a true pocket passer, whereas McDaniel thrived having Tua Tagovailoa throw with anticipation to spots. Either Herbert struggles to do both or McDaniel isn't putting him in a position to show that he can. I still think Herbert has good football in him, but that's harder to sell by the week. And your point about mismatched personnel is a good one.

True or false: J.J. McCarthy won't be the only QB traded before the deadline.
Graziano: True! A lot of these situations are going to change drastically by midseason. Jacoby Brissett could struggle and prompt the Cardinals to want to see third-round rookie Carson Beck, which could lead to Brissett or veteran backup Gardner Minshew II being dealt. We heard talk in the offseason about the Bears looking into trading Tyson Bagent, and maybe someone gets interested if he gets a start or two during Caleb Williams' absence and looks good.

We also heard about the Eagles dealing Tanner McKee, and they could still do so if they're comfortable with Andy Dalton as QB2. They could also deal Dalton. Joe Flacco is still in the league and always seems to appeal to someone, though I believe Cincinnati values him highly as a fallback should something happen to Joe Burrow. Could someone ask Jacksonville about Quinn Ewers or Nick Mullens?

Quarterbacks get hurt all the time and teams are always looking for them. The Giants just traded a fifth-round pick for a guy who couldn't beat out Kyler Murray or Carson Wentz in camp. Quarterbacks will definitely be moved.

Fowler: Brissett could be a valuable trade asset if the Cardinals want to look at Beck later in the season. And the Jaguars like Ewers, so perhaps Mullens is expendable. These are hardly slam dunks, but the landscape could foster movement. So, I'll set the over-under on the number of quarterbacks dealt at 2.5.

Three teams -- the Eagles, Browns and Steelers -- are carrying four quarterbacks and probably would welcome a deal at the right price. And more injuries at the position will cause more trade talk. We've already seen six established starters go down through the first three weeks. Kansas City sees QB2 upside with Garrett Nussmeier, so if there are trade inquiries for Justin Fields, perhaps the Chiefs take a look. Spencer Rattler (Saints) and Stetson Bennett IV (Rams) elicited trade interest in the preseason.

Graziano: A guy we don't hear much about anymore is Anthony Richardson Sr., and I still wonder if someone will throw a late-round pick at the Colts for a chance to salvage his talent. There was the whole kerfuffle in the offseason about him demanding a trade, but we never heard much about teams being interested in acquiring him. As the season goes on and the Colts get closer to the end of his rookie contract, maybe they're willing to take less to move on.

Fowler: The Giants never called Indianapolis about Richardson's availability, but my sense is that the Colts don't want to trade him right now. Perhaps that changes, but Richardson is QB2 despite neither he nor third-stringer Riley Leonard having particularly good camps. Richardson would welcome the chance to learn behind the scenes in the McVay or Shanahan trees, but that doesn't feel feasible, at least this season.

Graziano: I also wonder whether the Steelers will try to get something for Will Howard or Drew Allar, since it's hard to see them needing both moving forward. And the big one is probably Mac Jones. The 49ers have said they aren't interested in dealing him, and I believe it would take a lot to change their minds. But if someone gets desperate enough, who knows?

Fowler: It would take real draft capital -- perhaps a Day 2 pick -- to get in the door on Jones. Brock Purdy is playing at an MVP level, but he also sat out seven games last season, with Jones filling in admirably. San Francisco could be there at the end if its aging roster holds up, so it makes little sense to deal Jones right now.

Are people around the league buying the Raiders' 3-0 start?
Fowler: Yes ... to a point. The evaluators I've spoken with see an offense that's humming. "I have no reason to believe it is a fluke right now," one AFC executive said. Quarterback Kirk Cousins is tied for the league lead in touchdown passes (nine). Tight end Brock Bowers looked unguardable Sunday in New Orleans, wide receiver Tre Tucker is emerging and the 1-2 rushing combo of Ashton Jeanty and Mike Washington Jr. is promising. A once-maligned offensive line looks more cohesive.

On defense, new additions such as free agent linebacker Nakobe Dean and rookie defensive backs Treydan Stukes and Hezekiah Masses are paying off. So, the vibes are high in Vegas and the plan to develop Fernando Mendoza behind the scenes looks like a good one. But the early schedule was soft, and the Raiders knew they needed to start fast. Kansas City (Week 4), Buffalo (Week 6) and the L.A. Rams (Week 7) await. The next month will illustrate where the Raiders really are in their rebuild.

Graziano: Knowing Steve Spagnuolo the way we do, my anticipation is that the Chiefs will do whatever they can to take Bowers out of the game plan this week and force the Raiders to beat them with their wide receivers, which remain the question of the offense. Coach Klint Kubiak and the Raiders want to lean into two-tight-end and two-running-back sets because those positions are the strengths of the offense. We'll see what happens if a defense succeeds in making Las Vegas play left-handed, so to speak. But that's almost nitpicky in the big picture. The Raiders entered this season with no expectations, so to be 3-0 indicates that Kubiak has quickly succeeded in establishing some sort of culture on which to build.

Kubiak is doing an outstanding job. The offensive line is better than most people expected it to be (which probably highlights the failures of last season's Raiders coaching staff as much as anything), and the team is getting contributions from young guys on defense. Fifth-round rookie Masses was AFC Defensive Player of the Week in Week 2. Even if they can't continue the win streak, there has been enough good stuff for the Raiders to earn respect of people around the league, and it indicates they might be onto something long term. If nothing else, the goal of having a good-enough roster to support Mendoza when he's deemed ready seems very attainable.

Fowler: In hiring Kubiak, the Raiders were getting, at minimum, an improved offense with a skilled playcaller. It turns out his message is resonating, too. Word is Kubiak and minority owner Tom Brady really hit it off in the interview process over their love of football, talking about scheme and football life in detail. Kubiak's love for the game runs deep and is evident. He will face challenges in the future, like all coaches, but he seems to be pressing the right buttons so far.

It's no surprise that the Raiders have struck a true run-pass balance (93 carries to 92 passing attempts). That showed up with Kubiak's 2025 Seattle offense (507 rushes to 481 passes). I'm still not wholly convinced the Raiders' offensive line will hold up over 17 games, but a solid run game will improve its chances.

Graziano: Quite a turnaround for an organization that agreed to trade its best defensive player, Maxx Crosby, to the Ravens in March before Baltimore pulled out over concerns about Crosby's knee. Not only is Crosby playing like his old self, but he also sounds as if he's completely with the Kubiak program and has no desire to play anywhere else. What a benefit to a defense that's figuring out who its long-term contributors are going to be. It has been a fun start to Las Vegas' rebuild.

Which team's injury issues are most concerning?
Graziano: The easy answer is the 49ers, but they're 3-0 and deal with this every year, so I don't think it's them. Maybe the Giants? They've lost their starting quarterback and their top veteran edge rusher to season-ending injuries. It's hard to bounce back from that, especially when your roster wasn't exactly all the way filled out to begin with. I also don't know that people are sufficiently concerned about the Ravens already being down their top three preseason options at center and talking about rookie guard Olaivavega Ioane as a potential solution at the position after he had to finish Sunday's game there. Those jump immediately to mind.

Fowler: If San Francisco can survive the season with its core players remotely healthy, there's no reason why it can't be in the thick of the playoff race in January. The same probably goes for Baltimore.

As for other teams, the Panthers are down their top two corners, including Pro Bowl player Jaycee Horn for a significant portion of the season. Guard Damien Lewis is out because of an elbow issue. They lost pass rusher Nic Scourton in the preseason. Wide receiver Jalen Coker has been banged up. Both starting tackles from a year ago, Ikem Ekwonu and Taylor Moton, haven't played because of injury. Star linebacker Devin Lloyd sat out Week 3. Running back Jonathon Brooks is out six weeks. And, oh yeah, Bryce Young has lower-body soreness that he's getting checked out via a second opinion. The Panthers rebuilt the roster with a 2026 breakout in mind, but attrition is affecting that plan.

Graziano: I don't think the Patriots can match these teams for volume, and they seem to have plenty of issues right now independent of health. But it bears mentioning here that they're playing without top wide receiver A.J. Brown and the long-term injury to right guard Mike Onwenu, who's on IR because of a broken ankle, was the last thing this struggling offensive line needed.

Fowler: The NFC East is battered as a whole. The Giants and Commanders are without their starting quarterbacks, though Jayden Daniels will be back. As you pointed out, Dan, the Giants have lost two of their best players in quarterback Jaxson Dart and edge rusher Brian Burns. And injuries are mounting for Dallas, which is without linebacker DeMarvion Overshown, cornerback Cobie Durant, defensive lineman Jonathan Bullard and three safeties (P.J. Locke, Jalen Thompson, Malik Hooker). Dallas has the offensive firepower to contend, but its defense is ranked 30th in the NFL and has several holes that need to be backfilled.

The entire NFL injury scene seems out of whack, and perhaps it's no coincidence that lighter offseason practice schedules and lack of preseason reps are leading to more players being hurt, but that's a conversation for another time.

What is your best piece of fantasy football advice for this week?
Graziano: I'm trying to trade for Titans running back Tony Pollard in some leagues. A few people who've watched Tennessee play have singled out Pollard as someone who seems more explosive this season and is running well. The Titans are such a mess that it's possible Pollard's managers aren't considering him as a real week-to-week option.

He gets the Ravens this week, which sounds intimidating, but Baltimore has been middle-of-the-pack in rushing yards allowed and only two teams have given up more rushing touchdowns. Pollard's value might be lower than it should be, and in a league in which RB committees are all the rage, you could do worse as a weekly, set-and-forget RB2 option.

Fowler: Continuing on the running back front, I'd roster either Miami running back -- Ollie Gordon II or Jaylen Wright -- in the aftermath of the De'Von Achane injury. My sense is that Gordon and Wright will share the load in the short term, and Wright is expected to return from injury this week. One of the two could emerge over the next few weeks, but for now Miami plans to use both. Wright has big-play potential, while Gordon projects as more of an every-down back.

stories.headline: Schlittler and Rice torment hometown team as Yankees beat rival Red Sox 9-0 in playoff opener
stories.summary: — Cam Schlittler pitched another playoff gem against the Boston Red Sox, and Ben Rice also burned their hometown team with a late grand slam and six RBI as the New York Yankees opened this Wild Card Series rematch with a 9-0 victory Tuesday night.
stories.body:
NEW YORK -- — Cam Schlittler pitched another playoff gem against the Boston Red Sox, and Ben Rice also burned their hometown team with a late grand slam and six RBI as the New York Yankees opened this Wild Card Series rematch with a 9-0 victory Tuesday night.


With the Yankees minus star slugger Aaron Judge because of a calf injury, Rice homered twice, doubled and finished with four hits to power the offense. No. 9 batter Austin Wells drove in two runs for New York, and 21-year-old rookie George Lombard Jr. had three hits in his postseason debut.


Rice and Schlittler were both raised among Red Sox fans in Massachusetts and went to college in New England before getting plucked by the Yankees out of Boston's backyard in baseball's amateur draft.


Schlittler, a clear frontrunner for the AL Cy Young Award after leading the league with a 1.95 ERA, struck out 10 and walked one in 6 1/3 innings. He allowed only two hits while throwing 117 pitches — 10 more than his previous career high and most by a Yankees postseason starter since Hall of Fame lefty CC Sabathia threw 121 in the 2012 AL Division Series against Baltimore.


The major league high this season was 120 by Dylan Cease for Toronto at Boston in July.

stories.headline: Kessler talks up Lakers' title hopes behind 'nasty' defense
stories.summary: New addition Walker Kessler is convinced the Lakers have the right guys to be "a nasty defensive team" and a contender in the Western Conference this season.
stories.body:
EL SEGUNDO, Calif. -- The Los Angeles Lakers' offense has thrived since Luka Doncic arrived in 2025, but center Walker Kessler needed only one day of training camp to be convinced the team's defense will hold up its end of the bargain this season.

"Listen, I think we're going to be a nasty defensive team," Kessler said Tuesday. "I think people aren't taking into account how good our perimeter defense is going to be. A lot of guys are very smart on the perimeter and positionally can play really good defense. We have guys who are just ball hawks."

During JJ Redick's two seasons as coach, the Lakers have ranked above average in offensive efficiency and below average in defensive efficiency. After a transformative summer that saw the departure of LeBron James and several other veteran players, the Lakers are hoping to establish a more aggressive defensive identity with a rebuilt roster that includes Doncic, guard Austin Reaves, Kessler and a deep group of young wings.

Redick said Tuesday that his first goal during training camp was to "establish our defensive principles." With both forward spots in the starting lineup open for competition, Redick said he met with the team's wings last week to give them their marching orders.

"They understood the assignment today," he said. "That was exciting. They set the tone for us defensively. There was a lot of physicality, a lot of grabbing and holding, and a lot of disruption without gambling."

The 7-foot-2 Kessler, who was traded by the Utah Jazz to the Lakers this summer, will serve as the back-line rim protector after averaging 2.4 blocks per game during his first four seasons.

"The paint is kind of closed when [Kessler] is on the court," Doncic said.

From there, Doncic's remade supporting cast includes defensive specialists Jarred Vanderbilt and Matisse Thybulle as well as free agent additions Quentin Grimes, Sandro Mamukelashvili, Collin Sexton and Ziaire Williams. Kevon Looney, a veteran center who won two championships with the Golden State Warriors, will back up Kessler.

Kessler praised Looney for his "mind and positioning," Vanderbilt for his skill defending all five positions, and Thybulle, Grimes, Sexton and Williams for their ability to apply defensive pressure.

"Having those guys that can steal the ball ... [and] when they do get beat, be able to recover, it makes my job a lot easier," he said. "It's a lot easier to block a shot when a dude has someone on his hip instead of an open lane towards the basket."

The Lakers boasted the NBA's No. 3 defense when they won the 2020 championship and the No. 1 defense during the 2020-21 regular season. But their performance on that end has slipped noticeably in the years that followed.

Los Angeles fired Frank Vogel as coach after ranking 21st in defense during the 2021-22 season, then fired his successor, Darvin Ham, after ranking 17th in defense in 2023-24. The Lakers finished 20th on defense last season, their first full campaign after trading All-Star big man Anthony Davis to the Dallas Mavericks for Doncic.

Kessler was confident the Lakers "definitely can be a contender" in a Western Conference that includes title favorites with elite defenses such as the Oklahoma City Thunder and San Antonio Spurs.

"I think we have a lot of great tools and versatility," he said. "The guys are already getting along. Connection makes championship teams."
